common_name: Pink Temptation Turtlehead (Compact Seed-Strain Pink Turtlehead)

planting.note: Start seed indoors under lights 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once danger of frost has passed; as a true seed strain rather than a vegetatively propagated clone, this compact selection reliably flowers in its first season when started early.

directions: Introduced by Jelitto Perennial Seeds in 2006, this is one of the few turtleheads bred as a true seed strain rather than propagated only by division, meaning plants raised from seed come reliably true and can bloom the same year if started early indoors. It forms a tidy, dense mound only about a foot and a half tall and wide, noticeably shorter than the straight species, and is topped from late summer into fall with the same hooded, deep-pink, snapdragon-like flower spikes typical of pink turtlehead. Site it in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, such as along a shaded rain garden edge or stream bank, where its compact habit fits smaller beds better than taller wild-type clumps. Established plants can also be divided in spring to bulk up a planting once established.

common_name: Purple Turtlehead (Central U.S. Rose Turtlehead Variety)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring into consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil; this variety naturally occupies streambank and swamp-forest habitat across the central United States rather than the Southeast, so it tolerates cooler summers and heavier, wetter soils than typical Chelone obliqua stock.

directions: This botanical variety of rose turtlehead is native to wet streambanks and swamp forests of the central United States, from Minnesota and Iowa south to Missouri, Kentucky, and Arkansas, a distinctly more inland and northerly range than the Mid-Atlantic and Southeastern populations of typical Chelone obliqua. Its flower spikes lean toward deeper mauve-purple and lavender-rose tones rather than the straight species' cleaner pink, and it produces the same glossy, dark green, opposite leaves on upright, unbranched stems. Grow it in dappled shade to full sun with soil that never dries out, since it comes from perpetually saturated wetland margins and struggles wherever moisture is inconsistent. Bumblebees remain its primary pollinators, prying open the pinched, turtle-head-shaped flowers that give the genus its name.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Pink Lanterns Columbine (Compact Pink Wild Columbine Selection)

planting.note: Set out potted divisions or fall-stratified seedlings in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil once the soil has warmed in spring; this compact selection suits edging along shaded pathways or the front of a border better than the taller wild form.

directions: Discovered as a compact, mounded seedling at the Dyck Arboretum of the Plains in Kansas, this selection of native eastern columbine trades the species' typical red-and-yellow coloring for dainty pink, nodding blooms with pale yellow centers and short curving spurs, held on dark stems above blue-green foliage. It stays noticeably shorter and tighter than a wild-collected plant, and tends to open its first flowers slightly earlier in spring than most other columbine selections. Grow it in humus-rich, evenly moist soil with morning sun and afternoon shade, and expect the same short-lived but self-perpetuating habit as other Aquilegia canadensis selections, renewing itself through scattered self-sown seedlings. Its dwarf scale and early bloom make it a strong choice for hummingbirds and bees at the front of a woodland border.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil tolerant of both acidic and alkaline conditions, in full sun to partial shade; Prodigy was selected for a denser, more rounded crown and heavier bloom than typical seed-grown fringetrees.

directions: Selected and introduced by Select Trees of Georgia, this clonal cultivar was chosen from seedling stock for foliage that stays darker, glossier, and more resilient through summer heat than typical straight-species fringetrees, holding its health and color better into late summer. Its rounded, densely branched crown produces an especially heavy cloud of the species' signature drooping, fragrant, white fringe-like flower clusters in spring, often before the leaves have fully expanded. Reaching a modest 10 to 15 feet at maturity, it stays proportionate to smaller residential lots and foundation plantings where a full-sized wild fringetree might eventually crowd the space. It adapts to both acidic and alkaline soils and turns a clear yellow in fall, adding a second season of interest beyond its spring bloom.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this patented selection flowers heavily even as a young, newly transplanted tree.

directions: Patented under U.S. Plant Patent PP36,524, this cultivar arose as a chance seedling discovered in 2021 among a field of more than 200 unnamed Chionanthus virginicus grown at a South Carolina nursery, and was later propagated and evaluated in Georgia's Piedmont region. It opens its slightly spicy-scented, strap-petaled white flowers in early to mid-April, earlier than many seedling-grown fringetrees, and blooms prolifically even while still young rather than needing years to reach flowering maturity. Its habit is upright and oval with a dense canopy of glossy dark green leaves that eventually grows into a substantial specimen tree well over 15 feet tall, larger at maturity than the more compact Emerald Knight or Spring Fleecing selections. No particular disease or pest susceptibility has been noted for this selection during evaluation.
sources: U.S. Patent and Trademark Office - Plant Patent PP36,524
